t: How to build a consistent sleep routine
text:
Regular sleep and wake times help your body clock. Here is how to build a routine that sticks.
Good sleep supports your mood, focus, memory and physical recovery. Most adults need at least 7 hours a night, and teenagers usually need 8 to 10 hours.
## Simple habits that help
- Wake up at about the same time every day, including weekends.
- Give yourself 30–60 minutes to wind down: dim the lights, read, or stretch gently.
- Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
- Put screens away before bed and avoid caffeine late in the day.
- Get daylight and some movement during the day.
## When to talk to a doctor
If you often struggle to sleep, feel very tired during the day even after enough rest, or someone notices you snore loudly or stop breathing in your sleep, talk to a doctor.

t: Balanced eating: what goes on a healthy plate
text:
A healthy diet is about regular patterns, not strict rules. A few simple targets go a long way.
Healthy eating is less about strict rules and more about everyday patterns. The World Health Organization highlights a few simple targets for adults.
- Eat at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day — about five portions.
- Keep free sugars below 10% of your daily energy; even less brings extra benefits.
- Keep salt under 5 g a day — roughly one teaspoon.
- Choose whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts and unsaturated oils more often.
## Easy ways to start
- Fill half your plate with vegetables or fruit.
- Swap sugary drinks for water.
- Taste your food before adding salt.
- Plan a few simple meals ahead for busy days.
Needs differ with age, activity and health conditions. A doctor or registered dietitian can give personal advice.

Why water matters, how much to aim for, and easy ways to drink enough.
Water helps control your body temperature, supports digestion and keeps you alert. A common guide is about 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day.
You may need more in hot weather, during long physical activity, or when you are ill or recovering.
## Simple tips
- Keep a refillable bottle with you.
- Have a drink with every meal.
- Water, milk and unsweetened drinks all count; limit sugary drinks.
- Drink a little more on active or hot days.

Stress is normal, but it can pile up. Small daily actions can make a real difference.
Stress is a natural reaction to pressure. When it builds up, it can affect your sleep, mood and concentration — but small daily steps can help.
- Move your body: activity can calm strong emotions and clear your head.
- Focus on what you can control, and take one small step.
- Connect with friends, family or classmates.
- Make regular time for yourself.
- Avoid relying on caffeine, alcohol or smoking to cope.
- At the end of the day, write down three things that went well.
## Getting support
If stress or low mood lasts for weeks, or you feel unable to cope, reach out to a doctor or a mental health professional. If you ever feel unsafe, seek urgent help straight away.

t: Iron, energy and anaemia: the basics
text:
What anaemia is, who is most at risk, and how food choices can support healthy iron levels.
Anaemia means the blood carries less oxygen than usual, often because there is too little haemoglobin. Women and girls who have periods, pregnant women and young children are among the groups most at risk.
## Signs people often notice
- Tiredness and low energy
- Feeling dizzy or faint
- Cold hands and feet
- Headaches
- Shortness of breath, especially during activity
## Everyday nutrition
Iron-rich foods include beans and lentils, leafy greens, eggs, fish and meat. Eating them with vitamin C foods such as citrus fruit or peppers can help your body absorb iron.
Only a blood test can confirm anaemia. Do not start iron supplements on your own — talk to a doctor if you notice these signs.

Many heart risks come from daily habits. These are the ones that matter most.
Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, and many of its risks come from everyday habits. The WHO names unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use and harmful use of alcohol as key behavioural risks.
- Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
- Eat more vegetables, fruit and whole grains, and less salt.
- Avoid smoking and keep alcohol low.
- Get regular health checks, including blood pressure.
A regular check-up can find risks early. Ask your doctor how often you should have one.

t: It's OK to talk: looking after your mental wellbeing
text:
Talking about how you feel is a strength. Simple ways to look after your mind.
Everyone has hard days. Talking about how you feel is a sign of strength, and it often makes problems feel more manageable.
- Tell one person you trust how you are really doing.
- Notice changes in your sleep, appetite or energy.
- Keep moving and stay in touch with others.
- Use trusted self-help tools, such as NHS Every Mind Matters.
If you feel unable to cope or to keep yourself safe, seek urgent help from emergency services or a crisis line in your country.

t: How much activity do children need?
text:
Guidelines for ages 5 to 18, with fun ways to help children move more.
For ages 5 to 18, guidelines suggest an average of at least 60 minutes of moderate or vigorous activity a day across the week.
- Mix it up: running games, cycling, swimming, dancing.
- Include activities that strengthen muscles and bones, like climbing or jumping.
- Break up long periods of sitting and screen time.
- Build up gradually, and use helmets and protective gear for cycling or skating.
Children with health conditions or disabilities can be active too — a doctor can help choose suitable activities.

t: How much sleep do we need at each age?
text:
Recommended sleep from toddlers to adults, and tips for calm bedtimes.
Sleep needs change as we grow. These are the recommended amounts per day:
- Toddlers (1–2 years): 11–14 hours, including naps
- Preschool (3–5 years): 10–13 hours, including naps
- School age (6–12 years): 9–12 hours
- Teens (13–17 years): 8–10 hours
- Adults (18–60 years): 7 hours or more
A calm, regular bedtime routine — a bath, a book, lights down — helps children settle. Keeping devices out of the bedroom at night helps too.

t: Staying active as you get older
text:
Daily movement helps older adults keep strength, balance and independence.
Being active every day helps older adults keep their strength, balance and independence. Even light activity is better than none.
- Move every day: walking, gardening, housework all count.
- On at least two days a week, do strength, balance and flexibility exercises, such as tai chi or chair exercises.
- If you can, aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
- Break up long periods of sitting.
Staying connected with others matters too. If you have not been active for a while or have a health condition, speak to a doctor before you start.

t: Moving more: a simple weekly plan
text:
How much activity adults need, what "moderate" means, and how to fit it in.
Adults are advised to do about 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus strength exercises on at least two days.
Moderate activity raises your heart rate — like brisk walking or easy cycling. Vigorous activity makes you breathe hard and fast, like running.
- Split it up: for example, 30 minutes on five days.
- Short bursts count: take the stairs, walk part of your journey.
- Pick activities you enjoy, so they last.
- Sit less and get up regularly.
src: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64 — NHS (https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/exercise-guidelines/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/)

text:
Why warming up and resting are part of training — not a break from it.
A short warm-up of at least six minutes — marching on the spot, knee lifts, shoulder rolls — prepares your muscles and joints for exercise.
- Increase effort gradually.
- Plan rest days: your body gets stronger while it recovers.
- Sleep well and drink enough water after training.
- Stop if you feel pain, dizziness or feel unwell.
More is not always better. Training hard without enough rest can lead to injury and tiredness.
